problems: stop 1 card 9, answer 3: copies a Prep line word for word

explanations.explanation: David opens with, "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want" — that is, he won't lack what he needs (Psalm 23:1). The word points to provision: with the Lord as shepherd, needs are met. It's a simple trust claim, not a promise of every luxury.

The verse doesn't say David must earn what he needs. It says, "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want" (Psalm 23:1), which speaks of God's provision, not a work-you-do-to-get-it idea. This line is about trust in the shepherd's care, not a paycheck.

David isn't saying he won't lose things. The psalm opens, "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want" (Psalm 23:1), which means he won't lack what he needs. The focus is provision and care, not the absence of loss.

The images — "green pastures" and "quiet waters" — point straight to rest and peace (Psalm 23:2). A shepherd who makes his sheep lie down and leads them to still water is setting them in safety and calm. This is the soothing picture David paints.
Those images don't fit hard work. "He makes me lie down in green pastures; He leads me beside quiet waters" (Psalm 23:2) paints rest and gentle care, not hustle. It's a restful scene, not a busy one.

The verse describes safe grazing and still waters, not immediate danger: "He makes me lie down in green pastures; He leads me beside quiet waters" (Psalm 23:2). If anything, it contrasts danger, showing provision and calm. It's a place of security.

David says, "He restores my soul" (Psalm 23:3). That word shows care going deeper than food and water — it means bringing the inner life back into health and wholeness. The shepherd's work includes renewal of the heart.
The verse doesn't say the Lord tests David's soul. It says, "He restores my soul" (Psalm 23:3), which is about renewal and healing. Restoration is the opposite of an exam.
David isn't saying God weighs his soul. The line reads, "He restores my soul" (Psalm 23:3), pointing to renewal and recovery. There's care and strengthening, not judgment by scales here.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His name
explanations.explanation: David says the LORD guides him "in the paths of righteousness for the sake of His name" (Psalm 23:3). That phrase shows God's guiding care reflects who God is and honors His reputation. It's about God's character and purposes, not the sheep's achievements.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His flock
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't give that reason. It reads, "...He guides me in the paths of righteousness for the sake of His name" (Psalm 23:3). The text points to God's name and honor, not primarily to the flock's benefit.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His land
explanations.explanation: That's not what the verse says. Psalm 23:3 reads, "...He guides me in the paths of righteousness for the sake of His name," focusing on God's name and character. The land isn't mentioned as the reason here.

explanations.answer: Because the LORD is with him
explanations.explanation: David says, "I will fear no evil, for You are with me" (Psalm 23:4). His confidence comes from God's presence in the dark valley, not from self-reliance. The shepherd's nearness removes fear.

David doesn't claim personal self-sufficiency. The verse says, "I will fear no evil, for You are with me" (Psalm 23:4), so his lack of fear is tied to God's presence, not his lone strength. It's the shepherd who keeps him steady.

The psalm doesn't say the valley is short. It says, "Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me" (Psalm 23:4). The reason for no fear is God's presence, not the valley's length.

David names the rod and staff as comfort: "Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me" (Psalm 23:4). Those shepherd's tools are signs of protection and guidance, and here they bring reassurance in the darkest place. The text says it plainly.

That's not what the verse says. Psalm 23:4 reads, "Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me," so David clearly finds comfort in the shepherd's rod and staff. The statement in the card is true according to the text.

David shifts to a hospitable picture and says, "You prepare a table before me" (Psalm 23:5). That shows the Lord as host who provides and honors his guest. It's a striking flip from pasture to banquet.
The verse doesn't use tent. It says, "You prepare a table before me" (Psalm 23:5), which is the image of a host welcoming a guest. Tent wouldn't match the feast picture here.
David didn't say bed. Psalm 23:5 uses a dining image: "You prepare a table before me." The emphasis is on being hosted and honored, not simply being given rest at night.

The verse actually says, "You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies" (Psalm 23:5), which means the table is prepared with the enemies there, not far away from them. So answering True would disagree with the text. The text places the feast openly, even with enemies present.

Correct — Psalm 23:5 says, "You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies." The image is of being honored openly, despite opposition. The table isn't set away from enemies; it's set before them.

When David says, "my cup overflows" (Psalm 23:5), he's using the overflowing cup to show abundance and generous blessing. The picture is of plenty, not lack. It's the host pouring so much the cup runs over.

The overflowing cup isn't about carelessness in this verse. Psalm 23:5 uses it as a sign of abundance: "my cup overflows." It's a blessing image, not a careless one. The text intends plenty, not spilling from neglect.
There's nothing about being rushed in the image. The line, "my cup overflows" (Psalm 23:5), describes abundance and generous provision. It doesn't convey hurry; it shows lavish blessing.

David closes saying, "Surely goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life" (Psalm 23:6). Those two words picture God's faithful blessings and steadfast love pursuing him through life. It's a confident hope rooted in the shepherd's care.

The verse doesn't promise wealth and honor. It reads, "Surely goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life" (Psalm 23:6), focusing on God's faithful kindness rather than material riches or status. The emphasis is God's presence and favor.

That's not what the text lists. Psalm 23:6 specifically names "goodness and mercy" as the things that follow him. Strength and wisdom are valuable, but the psalm highlights God's loving care and faithful kindness.

explanations.answer: In the house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: David ends, "and I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever" (Psalm 23:6). That expresses his hope to live in God's presence for all time. It's the final image of security and belonging under the shepherd's care.

The verse doesn't specify a human city. It says, "I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever" (Psalm 23:6), pointing to dwelling with God rather than a particular city like Hebron. The focus is presence with the Lord.

Psalm 23:6 doesn't say Canaan. It reads, "I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever," which speaks of being with God. The psalm's final hope is dwelling in the Lord's house, not a geographic land.
